clue.text: Modified electric door as this affected waterworks

indicators.note: modified means changed, so the letters of these three words are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tinkers with an electric door and finds themselves crying over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Modified' is the anagram signal: the fourteen letters of ELECTRIC DOOR AS are rearranged; 'this' just links the fodder to the definition. 'Waterworks' is slang for tears.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterworks is slang for weeping, and affected weeping is insincere sorrow, like the reptile said to weep while eating its prey.

clue.text: Not an ugly man, as a lecturer is

parts.note: a don is a university teacher or lecturer, especially at Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A tease that lecturers are handsome rather than plain.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's tail reads straight off as A DON IS; 'as' only links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this youth was so beautiful that his name became a byword for a handsome man.

clue.text: One follows councillor about to kill guide

indicators.note: follows means the word for one comes after the rest
about means surrounding, so the councillor's letters go round the word for kill

parts.note: to ice someone is slang for to kill them
taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: A guide is murdered after a councillor turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to kill' reads as a phrase of intent but is slang for murder; 'about' wraps the councillor round it, and 'follows' puts one at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A cicerone is a tour guide who shows sightseers round, named after the eloquent Roman orator.

clue.text: Part of France acquires a new starting point

indicators.note: acquires means takes in, so the region's name holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: Provence is a region of southern France

explanation.surface: A French region takes on a fresh beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'acquires' puts A and N inside PROVENCE, between the N and the C.
explanation.definitionFit: Provenance is the origin or source of something, such as the documented history of an artwork.

clue.text: Quick way to start with nothing

indicators.note: to start with places the word for nothing at the front, before the way

parts.note: FA is short for sweet FA, British slang for nothing at all
ST is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: Advice on how to begin from scratch, done quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet FA is British slang for nothing at all; 'to start with' puts it in front of the street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick and rapid are synonyms describing something that moves at speed.

clue.text: Radio presenter ought to get in after a couple

indicators.note: after means the following letters come behind the word a

parts.note: a DJ (disc jockey) presents music on the radio
ought is an old variant of aught, meaning nought or zero, giving O
taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: A radio presenter is told to get in after a couple of others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ought' looks like the verb of obligation but is a variant of aught, nought, so O. 'to get' only links; 'after' puts A first. The definition 'couple' is the verb, to join.
explanation.definitionFit: To couple and to adjoin both mean to join or be joined side by side.

clue.text: Stop chasing me, woman — I'm very old

indicators.note: chasing means the word for stop runs behind the word me

parts.note: taken as the word itself
an engine that dies stops working
Val is a woman's name, short for Valerie

explanation.surface: An old woman tells a pursuer to stop chasing her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chasing' puts the word for stop behind me. The definition speaks in the first person, as an object from the Middle Ages might.
explanation.definitionFit: Something from the Middle Ages is centuries old, so it can describe itself as very ancient.

clue.text: Awesome pair of bones

parts.note: rad is slang for excellent or awesome
II is two in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a splendid set of two bones.
explanation.walkthrough: II is two in Roman numerals; 'rad' is surfer slang for great.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is a forearm bone, and this is its plural.

clue.text: Be a student doctor with letter to send forward?

parts.note: to read a subject is to study it at university
ess is the spelt-out name of the letter S

explanation.surface: A medical student sends a letter onward.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'read' a subject is British for studying it at university; ESS is the name of the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail is forwarded by putting a new address on it, so sending it forward needs that.

clue.text: Truth accepted by royalist is distorted nicely

indicators.note: accepted by means the word for truth is taken into the rearranged letters
distorted means twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: a fact is a truth

explanation.surface: A royalist bends the truth in a pleasing way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distorted' rearranges the royalist's letters into SATISORILY, and 'accepted by' takes the truth in after the fifth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something nicely means doing it well enough to please, adequately and acceptably.

clue.text: Company investor isn't a silly tree-hugger

indicators.note: silly means foolish or muddled, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A company investor insists he is no daft environmentalist.
explanation.walkthrough: CO, then 'silly' rearranges the thirteen letters of INVESTOR ISN'T A.
explanation.definitionFit: Tree-hugger is a mocking name for a campaigner who protects nature and the environment.

clue.text: Disregards cuts

definitions.meaning: to discount something is to ignore it as unreliable

explanation.definitionFit: To discount a claim is to dismiss it, and discounts are reductions off a price.

clue.text: Unusual cargo ship takes on board a number of coffins

indicators.note: takes on board means loads aboard, so the letter is put inside the rearranged cargo ship
unusual signals that the letters of the two words appear in an odd order

explanation.surface: A freighter carries a strange load of coffins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a number of coffins' must be read together: the plural of a stone coffin. 'Unusual' rearranges the vessel's letters and 'takes on board' loads the A.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarcophagus is a stone coffin, and this is its plural, so several of them.

clue.text: Expensive new housing around Caribbean tourist spot

indicators.note: around means turned round, so the run of letters is read backwards
housing means holding inside, so the letters are found within these two words

explanation.surface: Costly new homes surround a Caribbean resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'housing' points to letters inside 'expenSIVE New', and 'around' reads them backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevis is an island in the Caribbean, part of the federation of St Kitts and Nevis, visited by holidaymakers.

clue.text: Fell down, only having last stand?

parts.note: in Thomas Harris's novel Hannibal, Hannibal Lecter hides in Florence under the alias Dr Fell

indicators.note: only having last means just the final letter of the word down is used

explanation.surface: Someone fell over and has only one stand left.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell' looks like a verb but is the alias Dr Fell used by Hannibal Lecter in Harris's novel Hannibal; 'only having last' takes N, the last letter of 'down'.
explanation.definitionFit: A lectern is a sloping stand from which a speaker or reader reads.

clue.text: Vehicle carrying drill, possibly iron, in picture

indicators.note: carrying means holding inside, so the vehicle's letters surround the others

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
a drill is a kind of baboon, loosely an ape, and possibly marks it as an example
Fe is the chemical symbol for iron

explanation.surface: A car carries a power drill and maybe an iron in a photograph.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drill' is not the tool but the West African baboon, which 'possibly' allows as an ape; 'carrying' puts it and iron inside the vehicle, before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture is a film, and this is the title of a thriller filmed in 1962 and remade by Scorsese in 1991.

clue.text: German measles problem, every drug rejected

parts.note: rub means a problem, as in 'there's the rub'

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the words for every and drug are read backwards together

parts.note: all and every both mean the whole number
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: German measles is a problem, and all drugs have been turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: E is crossword shorthand for ecstasy; 'rejected' turns the words for every and drug round together to make ELLA.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubella is the medical name for the mild viral illness commonly called German measles.

clue.text: We're good girls and line up in mostly best clothes

indicators.note: clothes is a verb here, meaning wraps round, so the shortened word surrounds the others
mostly means most of the word but not all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: taken as the word itself
a row is a line

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word in is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: taken as the word itself

explanation.surface: Well-behaved girls queue up dressed in their Sunday best.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clothes' is a verb, wrapping round; 'mostly' trims BES; 'up' turns the word in upwards to NI in this down entry. Brownies are junior Girl Guides, who speak the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Brownies are the junior branch of the Girl Guides, known for good deeds and good behaviour.

clue.text: Hobbyhorse to select — tail missing

parts.note: taken as the word itself

indicators.note: tail missing means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: to pick is to select

explanation.surface: Choosing a hobbyhorse whose tail has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail missing' drops the K from PICK; a hobbyhorse here is a favourite subject, not the toy.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobbyhorse is a favourite subject someone keeps returning to, a pet theme of conversation.

clue.text: Xmas Mass in brothel? Nothing to add

indicators.note: in means the letter for Mass goes inside the slang word

parts.note: crib is old slang for a brothel
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A shocking question about holding a Christmas Mass in a brothel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts M inside CRIB, and the O for nothing is added at the end. Crimbo is British slang for Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal short names for Christmas, one written and one British slang.

clue.text: I'm referring to turnover within European budget?

definitions.text: I'm referring to turnover within European budget?

indicators.note: within means the reversed letters sit inside the other two pieces

parts.note: to budget a project is to cost it

indicators.note: turnover means the words for I'm and referring to are read backwards together

parts.note: I'm gives the letters IM
on means about or referring to, as in a talk on taxes

explanation.surface: Someone talks about sales turnover inside an EU budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turnover' reverses I'm and the word for referring to as one unit, giving NOMI; 'within' sets that inside the euro piece and the budget word. The whole clue describes what such a person discusses.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialist in the science of money, trade and markets would talk about turnover and budgets.

clue.text: Yuppie's last girlfriend about to support one's fancy?

indicators.note: to support in a down clue means the following letters sit below the I

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I; the 's is a link

indicators.note: about means the girlfriend's letters go round the letter

parts.note: a date is a girlfriend one goes out with

indicators.note: last means only the final letter of the word yuppie is used

explanation.surface: A yuppie's latest girlfriend backs one's whim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last' takes E from 'Yuppie's'; 'about' puts DATE round it (DEATE); 'to support' sets that below I in a down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy something is to imagine it, and to ideate is to form an idea in the mind.

clue.text: Just in fun, one heard about deadly combat

indicators.note: in means the word for just goes inside the rearranged letters
about means around and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: fair and just both mean even-handed

explanation.surface: A man protests that he was only joking when people heard about a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' looks like the verb of the surface, but 'about' rearranges it with the two words before it; 'in' slips the word for just inside.
explanation.definitionFit: French for a matter of honour, this was a formal duel fought to settle an insult, often to the death.

clue.text: Zombie village's satanic resident

indicators.note: resident means living inside, so the letters lie within the words zombie village's

explanation.surface: A devilish resident of a village of the undead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resident' points to letters living inside 'zombiE VILlage's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanic means devilish and wicked, the very nature of the devil.

clue.text: Knocked-off flashy jewellery that's uncoordinated

parts.note: a knock-off is a fake, a sham
bling is slang for flashy jewellery

explanation.surface: Fake flashy jewellery that has been carelessly put together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's' only links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Shambling describes a clumsy, awkward walk without coordination.

clue.text: Late for lunch, initially out of puff?

parts.note: ex means former, as the late does of someone past
to can mean for, as in a toast to the bride

indicators.note: initially means only the first letter of lunch is used

explanation.surface: Someone late for lunch arrives breathless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'puff' is the verb, to praise extravagantly, as in a puff piece; 'out of' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To puff a product is to praise it lavishly, so both mean to laud.
